chunks: In-circuit testing (ICT). The question: What is in-circuit testing (ICT)? What can it capture?
In-circuit test (ICT) checks a finished board by pressing a bed of spring-loaded pins onto test pads on the board. A tester then measures each part where it sits.
It finds shorts, opens, missing parts, wrong values and parts put in backwards, and it points to the exact part or connection at fault.
It is fast, but it checks the build, not whether the product works.
Think of the pin-art toy, where hundreds of pins press against an object. Here each pin touches one spot on the board.
The catch: side routes around the part skew a plain measurement. Imagine measuring flow through one pipe in a network.
If both ends of a neighboring pipe sit at the same water pressure, no water flows in it. The tester uses that trick, which is called guarding.
The tester drives A with V test and senses the current at B, which is held at virtual ground. The guard probe grounds node G.
Because B is also at 0 volts, R3 has no voltage across it and carries no current, and R2's current is diverted to ground, so the sensed current is exactly V test/R1.
Without the guard the tester would read 10 kilohms in parallel with 14. 7 kilohms, about 5. 95 kilohms.
Bed-of-nails fixture: the holder of spring pins matched to one board. Test pad: a small exposed copper pad where a pin touches a net (one set of points wired together).
Parallel path: another route for current around the part being measured.
Guarding: holding the middle of a side route at the same voltage as its far end, so no measuring current flows there.
Short and open: a short is a connection that should not exist, and an open is a missing one.
Measure a 10 kilohms resistor with a side route of 4. 7 kilohms plus 10 kilohms, which is 14. 7 kilohms. Without guarding, the tester sees the two in parallel: 10 x 14. 7 / 24.
7 = about 5. 95 kilohms, a 40 % error that fails a good part.
With the middle of the side route held at the same voltage as the far end, the side route carries no measuring current. The tester then reads the true 10 kilohms.
That is the whole idea.
"In-circuit test checks a populated board by contacting test points with a bed-of-nails fixture and measuring each component in place, using guarding so parallel paths don't corrupt the reading.
It finds shorts, opens, missing or wrong parts, wrong values and reversed polarity, and it points to the exact component.
It's very fast, seconds per board, but needs test points on the nets and a fixture that costs thousands, and it doesn't tell you whether the product functions."
